items.body:
### What happened?

When a workload is scaled down to 0 replicas (with KEDA for instance), the HPA controller attempts to calculate the average metric value (total metric / 0 replicas). This division by zero causes the HPA's `status.currentMetrics[0].external.current.averageValue` to underflow to `-9223372036854775808m`(math.MinInt64) and, if the scaling becomes then inactive, gets stuck with this underflow value in the HPA object.

### What did you expect to happen?

When the workload replica count is 0, skip the per-pod average calculation. The HPA controller should bypass the division step when statusReplicas == 0 and return the total raw metric value as a fallback.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?


- Configure an HPA with an External metric and target type AverageValue
- Scale the workload up to at least 1 replica so the HPA performs a metric evaluation
- Scale the workload down to 0 replicas
- Check the HPA status using kubectl get hpa (or -o yaml)

I have made a script to reproduce this with KEDA in https://gist.github.com/KengoA/65599c5ffd635c5e1c1c783502a7d340 which I ran on a GKE cluster. I have the full stdout from the script in the gist, but it gets into a state like the following (replicas is shown as 5 here when I printed the output but this becomes 0 after a few seconds):
```
NAME            READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
mock-workload   0/0     0            0           49s

NAME                            REFERENCE                  TARGETS                         MINPODS   MAXPODS   REPLICAS   AGE
keda-hpa-mock-workload-scaler   Deployment/mock-workload   -9223372036854775808m/1 (avg)   1         10        5          50s
----------------------
```


This is also reported in https://github.com/kedacore/keda/issues/5730 with other users facing a similar issue, and the overflow/underflow issue is identified by in https://github.com/kedacore/keda/issues/5730#issuecomment-2247692693.

### Anything else we need to know?

The zero division and then underflow issue seems to happen on GKE clusters which I replicated above. I saw moments of overflow during transient phases.

Note that this does not affect the autoscaling behaviour itself as this only happens when replica is 0.

This is an umbrella issue to track required changes prior to beta promotion of InPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption (KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5836)

It is a combination of the initial beta criteria we scoped out on https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5836, as well as important considerations identified during code review of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000.

### KEP Beta Criteria
- [ ] Define and implement relevant metrics and events.
- [ ] Define, implement, and link additional comprehensive integration tests in the KEP.
- [ ] Clarify and design co-existence mechanics for workload-aware scheduling (e.g., group-wide coordinated preemption or evaluating pod group health before preempting).
- [ ] Address scenarios where a preemption victim's grace period exceeds the time window allocated for executing the resize operation (e.g., VPA's fallback time limit).
- [ ] Finalize the approach to prevent "double preemption" across scheduler restarts and long grace periods (e.g., evaluating `nominatedNodeName` vs. checking `spec.nodeName` in `DefaultPreemption`).
- [ ] Evaluate whether to solve the risk of additional unnecessary preemption by aligning `NodeResourcesFit` resource accounting logic with the Kubelet's logic (`max(desired, allocated, actual)`) when evaluating deferred pods.
- [ ] Ensure the Deferred resize scheduling cycle includes resources from `pod.status.nodeAllocatableResourceClaimStatuses` if KEP-5517 Alpha2 (DRA) is implemented.

### Implementation PR Follow-ups & Technical Items (PR #140000)
- [ ] **[Node Resources Fit Delta Calculation (`max(0, ...)` Handling)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000#discussion_r3608175391):** Re-evaluate the `NodeResourcesFit` resource accounting delta logic when calculating a deferred pod's target resource footprint. 
- [ ] **[Observability & Autoscaler Integration](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000#discussion_r3613628887):** Surface scheduling preemption failure reasons (via Events, appending details/reasons to status conditions like `Deferred`, or updating `PodResizePending`) so users and possibly autoscaling controllers (like VPA) can determine why space could not be made. Ensure that kubelet handles such changes (including consideration for version skew). 
- [ ] **[Binding Phase Refactoring](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000#discussion_r3609589583):** Evaluate progressing deferred pods through the binding cycle (implementing `Bind()` and updating `PodResizePending`) instead of using `Permit` phase rejections while waiting for Kubelet actuation. This removes waiting pods from the scheduling queue and allows eliminating unnecessary `ScaleUp` queueing hints in `NodeResourcesFit` [(discussion on ScaleUp QHints)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000#discussion_r3609619666).
- [ ] **[Framework Extension Point (`IsResponsible`)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000#discussion_r3609616086):** Evaluate introducing a general scheduler extension point interface (`IsResponsible(pod)`) to clean up runtime plugin execution and avoid individual `IsPodResizeDeferred(pod)` checks across multiple plugins.
- [ ] **[Integration Test Refactoring](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000#discussion_r3614974843):** Refactor new integration tests (`TestDeferredResizeNodePreemptionPolicy` and `TestDeferredResizeQueueingHandlers`) to be table-driven and consider reusing `CoreResourceEnqueueTestCase`.

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

### Description
When combining **Topology Aware Routing** (`service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto`) with the **HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA)**, there is a systemic architectural gap that risks localized pod starvation during scale-out events, and extreme endpoint imbalance during scale-in events. 

Currently, the HPA evaluates resource utilization (e.g., CPU, Memory) as a global, deployment-wide aggregate average. However, Topology Aware Routing deliberately isolates traffic to localized Availability Zones (AZs). 

This decoupled behavior creates a "Thundering Herd" trap during spikes, and a "Starvation" trap during downscaling, because the network routing layer is highly topology-aware while the autoscaling control loop is completely topology-blind.


### Why is this needed?


### Use Case
We run high-throughput microservices on AWS (EKS) distributed across 3 Availability Zones. To mitigate high cross-AZ data transfer costs ("Cross-AZ Tax") and lower network latency, we rely heavily on Topology Aware Routing. 

We face two distinct structural failures due to the lack of zone-aware autoscaling:

1. **The Scale-Out Trap (Localized Overload):** During localized network shifts or zone-specific traffic spikes, pods in a single AZ (e.g., `us-east-1a`) take 100% of that localized load. If `us-east-1a` pods hit 95% CPU utilization while pods in `us-east-1b` and `us-east-1c` remain idle at 10%, the cluster-wide average sits at ~38%. The HPA fails to trigger, and the pods in the stressed zone crash due to localized resource starvation.
2. **The Scale-In Trap (Zone Depletion):** When traffic drops globally and the HPA triggers a downscale event, the underlying ReplicaSet controller selects pods for termination without respecting zone distribution. It frequently terminates a disproportionate number of pods from a single zone. This leaves that specific zone entirely depleted of endpoints, breaking the path for subsequent localized traffic and forcing expensive, high-latency cross-AZ failovers.

### Proposed Solution / Architectural Approaches
We request native support for zone/topology-awareness within the core autoscaling and lifecycle framework:

1. **Topology-Aware Scale-Out Policy:** Introduce a configuration field in the HPA spec (e.g., `scalingPolicy.topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone`) that evaluates metrics per topology domain. If *any single zone* breaches the target utilization threshold, the HPA should proactively trigger a scale-up event.
2. **Topology-Aware Scale-In (Downscaling):** Ensure that when the HPA reduces the replica count, the scale-in mechanism balances pod terminations proportionally across all active topology domains. The controller must prevent downscaling from leaving a specific zone starved of healthy endpoints.
3. **Handling Soft Constraints (`ScheduleAnyway`):** If a deployment utilizes `whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway`, a Zone-Aware HPA should exploit this flexibility. During a localized spike, it should scale up replicas specifically within the hurting topology domain, allowing a temporary skew to absorb the traffic. During the subsequent scale-in event, the controller must prioritize deleting pods from the skewed zone to automatically return the cluster to its baseline balanced topology spread.

### Related Existing Issue
* **kubernetes/kubernetes #124149** 


### Additional Context
Current ecosystem workarounds require engineers to deploy entirely independent, duplicated Deployments and HPAs per AZ (e.g., `frontend-az-a`, `frontend-az-b`). This completely breaks standard GitOps principles, bloat CI/CD pipelines, and forces rigid, static replica constraints. Native lifecycle zone-awareness is required to bridge the gap between how Kubernetes routes traffic and how it manages compute capacity.

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Introduce an optional parameter to the HPA configuration, for example `backupReplicas`, that would allow you to:

- Specify the exact number of backup pods the autoscaler should maintain alongside the nominal ones.
- Better monitor the average load against the _TARGETS_ thresholds via the _kubectl get hpa_ command.

The new structure of the HPA specification would look like:

```go
type HorizontalPodAutoscalerSpec struct {
	ScaleTargetRef CrossVersionObjectReference
	MinReplicas *int32
	MaxReplicas int32
	Metrics []MetricSpec
	Behavior *HorizontalPodAutoscalerBehavior
	BackupReplicas *int32
}
```


### Why is this needed?

When a pod fails, Kubernetes might take time before restoring another pod on a new node. Deploying a new pod involves time-consuming operations like starting pod processes, downloading container images or sometimes waiting for an available node. Preprovisioning one or several shared backup pods in addition to the nominal ones can reduce the service interruption since those time-consuming operations are already achieved before the pod failure occurs.

Suppose that a Kubernetes service is configured to load balance flows onto a replicaset bound with an HPA defined with the `minReplicas` parameter equal to (_1_ + _Backup_) and with the `maxReplicas` parameter equal to (_Nominal_ + _Backup_). For the shared protection to be efficient, the HPA should add a (_x_ + _1_)<sup>th</sup> pod in the replicaset as soon as the pods are loaded at a ratio (_x_ - _Backup_) / _x_ that depends on _x_, the number of pods already deployed.

Based solely on fixed _TARGETS_ thresholds, the current `v2` HPA version does not satisfy this requirement. By introducing the optional `backupReplicas` parameter, the HPA can decide to add or remove a pod at the right pod load ratio and in this way become fully compatible with the shared protection requirement.

items.body:
### What happened? ### TL;DR on the Issue The HPA controller's selector overlap check ([`hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L396-L422)) runs every reconciliation for every HPA and holds a [global exclusive mutex](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L398-L399) while performing O(H) work. Despite starting [multiple worker goroutines](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L217), only one can execute the overlap check at a time. At scale, **_mutex contention_** dominates wall-clock time and reconciliation cannot keep up with the resync period. ### Mutex profile **60-second sample:** ``` File: kube-controller-manager Type: delay Duration: 60.02s, Total samples = 1.35hrs (8111.81%) 1.35hrs 100% sync.(*Mutex).Unlock 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).computeReplicasForMetrics 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector (99.41%) 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).validateAndParseSelector (99.92%) ``` 1.35 hours of goroutine-blocked time accumulated in 60 seconds of wall clock (8111% of wall clock duration). **Cumulative snapshot (since process start):** ``` File: kube-controller-manager Type: delay Total samples = 4.18hrs 4.18hrs 99.90% sync.(*Mutex).Unlock 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector (99.25%) 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).validateAndParseSelector (99.80%) ``` 99.25% of all mutex contention in the HPA controller is in `hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector`. ### Root cause Three problems compound: #### 1. Global exclusive lock on a per-HPA operation The [`hpaSelectorsMux`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L125) is held for the [entire body](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L398-L399) of `hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector`. This includes iterating all pods, inserting each into the BiMultimap, querying associations, and cleaning up. All worker goroutines contend on this single lock regardless of namespace. #### 2. BiMultimap cache is always cold [`KeepOnly([]Key{})`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L415) destroys all temporary pod entries at the end of every call. This triggers [refCount decrement to zero](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L188-L191), which deletes the `selectingByLabeled` cache entry. Every subsequent call hits the ["Cache miss. Scan selecting objects"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L138) path, iterating all HPA selectors in the BiMultimap. #### 3. A read operation implemented as write-query-delete The overlap check only needs to answer: "which existing HPA selectors match these pod labels?" That's a read query. But because the BiMultimap API currently supports "insert a labeled object, then ask who selects it," the code must [temporarily insert pods](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L403-L404) (a write), [query](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L406), then [delete](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L415). The writes require an exclusive lock, making concurrent execution impossible. Additionally, the BiMultimap is global across all namespaces, so [`Put` scans all selectors](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L143-L149) and [skips non-matching namespaces](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L144) , wasted iteration. #### Secondary effect: unbounded memory growth -> OOM The informer [resyncs all HPA objects](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L172) every 15s, delivering H update events to [`enqueueHPA`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L174) via the informer's [`processorListener.run()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L1330). When `enqueueHPA` [blocks on `hpaSelectorsMux`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L275), the listener stalls. The [`pop()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L1296) goroutine continues buffering incoming events into [`pendingNotifications`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L1223-L1225) , an unbounded ring buffer that [doubles when full](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/vendor/k8s.io/utils/buffer/ring_growing.go#L81-L83) and never shrinks. Each resync cycle delivers H more events; if the handler can't drain faster than events arrive, memory grows without bound. Heap profile diffs (~12 hours apart) confirm constant growth: ``` 2444.07MB k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache.(*sharedIndexInformer).OnUpdate 2016MB k8s.io/utils/buffer.(*TypedRingGrowing[...]).WriteOne ``` ### Time Complexity analysis Per single reconciliation, `bimap.Put()` hits a cache miss and [scans all `selectingObjects`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L138-L149) , O(H) iteration (the BiMultimap is global across namespaces). A full reconciliation cycle of all H HPAs, serialized by the exclusive lock, performs: ``` H reconciliations × O(H) per reconciliation = O(H*H) total ``` Doubling HPAs quadruples wall-clock time. ### What did you expect to happen? Workers should execute overlap checks concurrently as much as possible. The overlap check is fundamentally a read query ("which HPA selectors match these pod labels?") and should not require exclusive locking. #### Proposed solution Replace the BiMultimap + external mutex with a per-namespace selector map using `sync.RWMutex`: ```go type hpaSelectorStore struct { mu sync.RWMutex namespaces map[string]map[selectors.Key]labels.Selector } func (s *hpaSelectorStore) HPAsMatchingPods(namespace string, pods []*v1.Pod) []selectors.Key { s.mu.RLock() defer s.mu.RUnlock() uniqueLabels := make(map[string]labels.Set) for _, pod := range pods { key := labels.Set(pod.Labels).String() if _, seen := uniqueLabels[key]; !seen { uniqueLabels[key] = labels.Set(pod.Labels) } } hpas := make(map[selectors.Key]struct{}) for _, set := range uniqueLabels { for key, sel := range s.namespaces[namespace] { if sel.Matches(set) { hpas[key] = struct{}{} } } } return keys(hpas) } ``` ^^^ - `HPAsMatchingPods` uses `RLock`, all workers proceed concurrently. No temporary pod insertion, no cleanup, no cache to destroy. - only iterates selectors in the relevant namespace (HPA's in namespace), not all H. No cross-namespace scanning. - same effective optimization as BiMultimap's label cache (identical labels matched once), without write-then-destroy overhead. - HPA registration and selector updates acquire exclusive lock for a single map write, only on HPA create/update events, not per reconciliation. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Run the HPA controller at scale (10K+ HPAs) and collect a mutex profile: ```bash curl -s "http://localhost:10257/debug/pprof/mutex?debug=1" > mutex.pb.gz go tool pprof -text mutex.pb.gz ``` Contention in `hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector` will dominate as HPA count increases. ### Anything else we need to know? I did benchmarking with above solution and found significant improvement. Below are the results. #### Benchmark results 10,000 HPAs, 100 pods/HPA, 10 namespaces, 96-core machine. **Throughput (reconciliations/second):** | Workers | Current (BiMultimap) | Proposed (SelectorStore) | Speedup | |---------|---------------------|------------------------|---------| | 50 | 2,635 | 444,671 | 169× | | 100 | 2,600 | 506,873 | 195× | Current throughput **degrades** with more workers (increased contention). Proposed throughput **scales** with workers until CPU saturation. **Contention (100 workers):** | | Avg lock wait per operation | |---|---| | Current | 38.2 ms | | Proposed | 0.178 ms | | Reduction | **214×** | **Memory:** | | Bytes/HPA (10 namespaces) | Bytes/HPA (100 namespaces) | |---|---|---| | Current | 474 | 474 | | Proposed | 226 | 131 | **Allocations per operation (100 workers):** | | Bytes/op | Allocs/op | |---|---|---| | Current | 6,148,911 | 71,303 | | Proposed | 563,203 | 30,100 | #### Impact With 100 workers and 15s resync period: - **Current**: 2,600 ops/s → workers spend 99.7% of time blocked on the mutex. Selector overlap check alone consumes seconds of wall clock per cycle. - **Proposed**: 500K+ ops/s → selector check becomes negligible. ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version sh-5.2$ kubectl version Client Version: v1.34.0-beta.0-eks-7ffece0 Kustomize Version: v5.6.0 Server Version: v1.34.7-eks-40737a8 ```

items.body:
### What happened?


When using an External metric with `AverageValue` target, the HPA unintentionally scales up `spec.replicas` during rolling updates, even when the metric value indicates no scaling is needed.

During a rolling update, `status.replicas` temporarily exceeds `spec.replicas` due to surge pods. The HPA's tolerance check uses `statusReplicas` as both the divisor for ratio calculation and the return value when within tolerance. This causes `spec.replicas` to drift upward to match `status.replicas` without any actual load increase.

### Additional context

- The issue is most visible with tight `minReplicas`/`maxReplicas` ranges where even a +1 drift is significant
- Metric types using `Value` (not `AverageValue`) go through `GetExternalMetricReplicas` which has the same pattern and is likely affected as well
- The drift is bounded by `maxReplicas`, but causes unnecessary resource consumption and can interact poorly with custom controllers that set metric values based on `spec.replicas`

### Cascading impact: Cluster Autoscaler node thrashing

This bug can escalate from a pod-level issue to an infrastructure-level issue when combined with the Cluster Autoscaler (CA).

Consider the following scenario:

1. The Cluster Autoscaler decides to scale down a node (the node is underutilized)
2. Pods on the draining node enter `Terminating` state; replacement pods are scheduled to other nodes
3. During this transition, `status.replicas` temporarily exceeds `spec.replicas` (terminating pods + replacement pods both count toward status)
4. The HPA tolerance bug triggers: `spec.replicas` is bumped upward (e.g., 22 → 23)
5. This creates an **unexpected extra pod** that was not part of the original capacity plan
6. If the remaining nodes don't have enough capacity for this extra pod (since CA was in the process of *removing* a node, not adding one), the pod goes `Pending`
7. The `Pending` pod triggers the Cluster Autoscaler to scale **up** a new node

**Net result: A node scale-down operation triggers an unintended node scale-up.** The cluster oscillates — CA removes a node, HPA creates an extra pod, CA adds a node back — wasting infrastructure resources and causing unnecessary scheduling churn.

This is particularly impactful in environments with:
- Large pod resource requests (where a single extra pod can exceed remaining node capacity)
- Tight node capacity planning (nodes are close to full)
- Slow node provisioning (minutes of `Pending` state before the new node is ready)

### What did you expect to happen?

When the metric-derived ratio falls within the tolerance zone, the HPA should preserve the current `spec.replicas` (no scaling action), regardless of the transient `status.replicas` value.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

**Setup:**

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  minReplicas: 22
  maxReplicas: 24
  metrics:
  - external:
      metric:
        name: my_custom_metric
      target:
        averageValue: "1"
        type: AverageValue
    type: External
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: my-deployment
```

**Steps to reproduce:**

1. Deployment is stable: `spec.replicas = 22`, `status.replicas = 22`
2. External metric controller exposes metric value = 22 (meaning: 22 replicas desired, 1 per pod matches target)
3. Trigger a rolling update (e.g., change container image)
4. During rollout, `status.replicas = 23` due to maxSurge (surge pod created before old pod terminates)
5. HPA evaluates: `usageRatio = 22 / (1 × 23) = 0.957` → within 10% tolerance
6. HPA returns `statusReplicas = 23` as desired count
7. `23 > spec.replicas(22)` → **HPA patches spec.replicas to 23** (unintended scale-up)
8. Next cycle: `spec = 23`, `status = 24` (new surge) → same pattern → **spec drifts to 24**
9. Stops at `maxReplicas = 24`

**Observed: `spec.replicas` escalated 22 → 23 → 24 with zero load increase.**

### Anything else we need to know?

### Root Cause Analysis

In `GetExternalPerPodMetricReplicas` (and `GetObjectPerPodMetricReplicas`):

```go
replicaCount = statusReplicas  // ← uses status, not spec
usageRatio := float64(usage) / (float64(targetUsagePerPod) * float64(replicaCount))
if !tolerances.isWithin(usageRatio) {
    replicaCount = int32(math.Ceil(float64(usage) / float64(targetUsagePerPod)))
}
```

When `usageRatio` is within tolerance, `replicaCount` remains as `statusReplicas`. The calling code in `reconcileAutoscaler` then compares this with `scale.Spec.Replicas`. During rolling updates, `statusReplicas > specReplicas`, so the "no change needed" decision becomes an unintended scale-up.

The tolerance zone is designed to mean **"current state is acceptable, don't change"**, but the implementation effectively means **"align spec to status"**.

This is symmetric — the reverse case also applies:

| Transient state | Effect |
|----------------|--------|
| `status > spec` (rolling update surge) | Tolerance returns status → **unintended scale-up** |
| `status < spec` (pods still starting) | Tolerance returns status → **unintended scale-down** |

### Affected code paths

- `pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go`:
  - `GetExternalPerPodMetricReplicas()` — External metrics with AverageValue
  - `GetObjectPerPodMetricReplicas()` — Object metrics with AverageValue

### Suggested fix

When within tolerance, return `specReplicas` instead of `statusReplicas`:

```go
func (c *ReplicaCalculator) GetExternalPerPodMetricReplicas(
    statusReplicas int32,
+   specReplicas int32,
    targetUsagePerPod int64,
    ...
) (...) {
    // ... fetch and sum metrics ...

-   replicaCount = statusReplicas
+   replicaCount = specReplicas
    usageRatio := float64(usage) / (float64(targetUsagePerPod) * float64(statusReplicas))
    if !tolerances.isWithin(usageRatio) {
        replicaCount = int32(math.Ceil(float64(usage) / float64(targetUsagePerPod)))
    }
    // ...
}
```

Note: `statusReplicas` should still be used as the **divisor** in the ratio calculation (it correctly reflects actual load distribution). Only the **return value** when within tolerance should use `specReplicas` (preserving the user's desired state).

If someone has a custom resource which does not create pods but does have a scale subresource, it would be nice to be able to scale it based only on a custom metric. Currently this is not possible with HorizontalPodAutoscaler since it needs to list pods and does not just trust what the scale subresource tells it.

This would mean ignoring the implementation details of whatever the custom resource controller creates under the hood and just use the status of the scale subresource.

We recently introduced a new testing framework in #136799 that enables testing HPA behavior using an External Metrics mock server.

Currently, the framework includes only a single test case (basic scale up and scale down), which is not sufficient to fully validate HPA behavior. We should expand the test coverage to ensure the framework works reliably across more realistic scenarios.

We propose adding the following test cases:

- [ ] Multiple Metrics: Verify that a single HPA can correctly handle two or more external metrics simultaneously.
- [ ] Stabilization Window: Ensure that the HPA does not scale too aggressively when metric values fluctuate rapidly, respecting the configured stabilization window.
- [ ] Scaling Limits: Validate that the configured scaling limits (behavior.scaleUp and behavior.scaleDown) are enforced correctly.

Although #131091 was intended to enable the HPA e2e tests to run in parallel, it appears that they are still running serially. According to the [test-infra](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-autoscaling/sig-autoscaling-config.yaml#L386) configuration , the autoscaling tests are not currently executed in parallel.

According to @maxcao13, downstream (e.g., OpenShift) environments that attempted to remove the serial labels saw all 31 HPA tests run concurrently, leading to resource exhaustion and broken tests.

It’s currently unclear what the expected upstream behavior or outcome should be - whether the HPA tests are meant to run fully in parallel or only partially, depending on infrastructure capacity. Another possible approach could be to trim down the resources that each HPA test uses, allowing more tests to run concurrently without overwhelming the cluster.

Finally, my questions are:

items.body:
As the [KEP for PodLevelResources](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2837) evolved, it included accomodation for how its forward-looking API and behaviors will integrate with the existing container-specific resources APIs and behaviors (e.g., determining that pod-level resources take precedence; ref: https://github.com/ndixita/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-node/2837-pod-level-resource-spec/README.md#podspec-validation-rules).

Now that DRA is GA, and PodLevelResources are slated for beta in 1.34, we should fully flesh out the cooperative story here between the two. We can start with simply "what do we do when a pod spec includes both a pod-level resource configuration, and includes resource claims for one or more of its containers?".

It will probably make sense to update https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2837 with our conclusions, and prioritize any needed implementation work, to optimize for a smooth graduation of PodLevelResources to GA.

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

With k8s 1.34, `PodLevelResources` will allow users to specify resources on Pod level instead of on Container level. More info on how this works in the [KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2837)

This is a placeholder/umbrella issue, similar to VPA's https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler/issues/7571

### Why is this needed?

HPA needs to be able to correctly calculate the resources requested by a pod, when it's defined at pod or container level. Today, it calculates the pod requests by aggregating the requests of all containers within a pod: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/988cf21f0975cf95444a619481c13d2503d8ec6a/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L452-L475

We could use https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/988cf21f0975cf95444a619481c13d2503d8ec6a/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/resource/helpers.go, to calculate the pod requests in HPA.

items.body:
### What happened?

We are currently running several applications that are configured with metric-based scaling. These applications are expected to scale frequently in response to varying traffic patterns.

Occasionally, we observe the following error during scaling events (though it is not frequent), and there is no noticeable impact on the actual scaling process:

```
reason: FailedRescale, New size: <size>; reason: All metrics <below>/<above> target; error: Operation cannot be fulfilled on deployments.apps: the object has been modified; please apply your changes to the latest version and try again.
```

Our understanding is that this occurs due to a race condition where another controller or a CI/CD process is simultaneously patching or updating the Deployment object at the same time the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) attempts to scale it.

**In some cases, we observed the issue occurring even when there were no apparent changes to the Deployment object itself. Only a possible update to the resourceVersion, which we were unable to confirm the reason for the same**


To be cautious, we have set up an alert to notify us if the HPA fails to scale a deployment for any reason. However, encountering this specific error results in unnecessary noise and false positives in our alerting system.

### What did you expect to happen?

We expect the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) to perform retries internally and suppress the reporting of this error, as its occurrence generates unnecessary noise and may cause undue concern regarding system scaling.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To reproduce the issue:

- Configure a Deployment and Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) with CPU or memory-based scaling.
- Apply load to the Deployment pods to trigger scaling by the HPA.
- Simultaneously, perform multiple consecutive patch operations on the Deployment.

This sequence will result in the HPA reporting the same error in its events.

items.title: Sched Framework: Request to expose NodeInfo to PreFilter plugins and Score plugins

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: sig/autoscaling

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

In #119987 and #121954, the scheduling framework introduced `NodeInfo` as a parameter in the `RunPreScorePlugins` and `RunScorePlugins` functions of the `PluginsRunner` interface. Thank @Huang-Wei and @AxeZhan for these improvements that have made the framework easier to use. However, `NodeInfo` is still not exposed to the functions of the `ScorePlugin` and `PreFilterPlugin` interfaces (see [relevant code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/pkg/scheduler/framework/interface.go#L929)), which remains inconvenient for plugin users like [Koordinator](https://github.com/koordinator-sh/koordinator).

For instance, Koordinator aims to support [directive preemption](https://github.com/koordinator-sh/koordinator/blob/main/docs/proposals/scheduling/20220609-resource-reservation.md). To achieve this, it has had to propose [specific extensions](https://github.com/koordinator-sh/koordinator/blob/main/docs/proposals/scheduling/20220513-enhanced-scheduler-extension.md) to construct `NodeInfo` with reserved resources during the scheduling cycle.

Currently, while the `RunScorePlugins` function of the `PluginsRunner` interface accepts `NodeInfo` as a parameter, it does not pass it directly to the individual `Score` plugins. The relevant interface definitions are as follows:

```golang
type ScorePlugin interface {
	Plugin
	Score(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, p *v1.Pod, nodeName string) (int64, *Status)
	ScoreExtensions() ScoreExtensions
}

type PreFilterPlugin interface {
	Plugin
	PreFilter(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, p *v1.Pod) (*PreFilterResult, *Status)
	PreFilterExtensions() PreFilterExtensions
}

type PluginsRunner interface {
	RunPreScorePlugins(context.Context, *CycleState, *v1.Pod, []*NodeInfo) *Status
	RunScorePlugins(context.Context, *CycleState, *v1.Pod, []*NodeInfo) ([]NodePluginScores, *Status)
	RunFilterPlugins(context.Context, *CycleState, *v1.Pod, *NodeInfo) *Status
	RunPreFilterExtensionAddPod(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, podToSchedule *v1.Pod, podInfoToAdd *PodInfo, nodeInfo *NodeInfo) *Status
	RunPreFilterExtensionRemovePod(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, podToSchedule *v1.Pod, podInfoToRemove *PodInfo, nodeInfo *NodeInfo) *Status
}
```

We propose exposing `NodeInfo` in the `ScorePlugin` and `PreFilterPlugin` interfaces to allow plugin developers to access and utilize node information more conveniently. This would greatly enhance the flexibility and functionality of plugin development.

The interface can be updated as follows:

```golang
type ScorePlugin interface {
	Plugin
	Score(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, p *v1.Pod, node *NodeInfo) (int64, *Status)
	ScoreExtensions() ScoreExtensions
}

type PreFilterPlugin interface {
	Plugin
	PreFilter(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, p *v1.Pod, nodes []*NodeInfo) (*PreFilterResult, *Status)
	PreFilterExtensions() PreFilterExtensions
}
```

### Why is this needed?

Just like PR #119987 mentioned:

> - consistent function signature - all use NodeInfo
> - unleash more potential to use scheduler framework natively w/o hacks

We aim to align with and enhance the upstream framework for the following reasons, and we believe this change will benefit both the Kubernetes community and third-party plugin developers:

1. **Consistency**: Ensure that all plugins, including `ScorePlugin` and `PreFilterPlugin`, use a consistent `NodeInfo` parameter to simplify plugin development and reduce errors from mismatched data structures.

2. **Enhanced Flexibility**: Exposing `NodeInfo` directly allows plugin developers to implement advanced scheduling logic without workarounds, promoting cleaner and more maintainable code.

3. **Eliminate Workarounds**: Projects like [Koordinator](https://github.com/koordinator-sh/koordinator) currently need custom extensions to construct `NodeInfo` with reserved resources. Direct exposure of the `NodeInfo` would eliminate these workarounds.

4. **Future-Proofing**: Aligning with the upstream framework ensures easier adoption of future Kubernetes scheduler enhancements.

Looking forward to your feedback and support!

### What happened?

One of our production pool cannot scale up when its metrics reached its threshold because all pods became all unready at that moment when there was a peak traffic. Dig into the source code, we found that HPA calculate the desired replica using the ready pod count so cause the recommend replica is always 0.
```
func (c *ReplicaCalculator) getUsageRatioReplicaCount(currentReplicas int32, usageRatio float64, namespace string, selector labels.Selector) (replicaCount int32, timestamp time.Time, err error) {
	if currentReplicas != 0 {
		if math.Abs(1.0-usageRatio) <= c.tolerance {
			// return the current replicas if the change would be too small
			return currentReplicas, timestamp, nil
		}
		readyPodCount := int64(0)
		readyPodCount, err = c.getReadyPodsCount(namespace, selector)
		if err != nil {
			return 0, time.Time{}, fmt.Errorf("unable to calculate ready pods: %s", err)
		}
		replicaCount = int32(math.Ceil(usageRatio * float64(readyPodCount)))
	} else {
		// Scale to zero or n pods depending on usageRatio
		replicaCount = int32(math.Ceil(usageRatio))
	}

	return replicaCount, timestamp, err
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Could you please help explain why to use the ready count and is there any way to refine the implement?

### What happened?

A pod that terminated was considered by the HPA controller to be at its target utilization.

The controller logic ([1](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ed9572d9c7733602de43979caf886fd4092a7b0f/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L106-L120), [2](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ed9572d9c7733602de43979caf886fd4092a7b0f/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L211-L223)) is such that, while scaling up, it conservatively considers that a pod for which we couldn't get the utilization metric from a metrics API are at their target utilization. (On scale down, the assumption is conservatively that the utilization is 0.)

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the controller to assume that a terminated pod has an utilization of 0.

This is [already correctly handled for pods that terminated with a failure](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ed9572d9c7733602de43979caf886fd4092a7b0f/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L383), but the case where a pod terminated successfully isn't handled.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a Deployment with pods that terminate (without a failure) and observe that an HPA targetting this Deployment will assume that terminated pods are at target utilization.

### Anything else we need to know?

Handling the case where the pod is terminated normally [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ed9572d9c7733602de43979caf886fd4092a7b0f/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L383) will fix this.

items.body:
### What happened?

Some external cloud providers such as Azure use a pass-through(direct server return) load balancer. This means that TCP connections are not terminated on the loadbalancer, but instead downstream in the kubernetes cluster.

ExternalTrafficPolicy Cluster configures load balancers to send traffic to any node in the cluster, even if the node is not running a pod that the traffic is destined to. From there kube-proxy routes the request to the pod (which could either be on the same or different node). 

In our case, when client sets up a long living TCP connection and that traffic path hits kube-proxy on a node that downscales sometime during the duration of the TCP connection, we observe 520 errors from the server. 

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubernetes nodes that act as a intermediate hop between the loadbalancer and the node/pod that the traffic is destined to should gracefully allow all existing TCP connections to finish before the node/processes are terminated. 

This is important because some loadbalancers like Azure continue to send traffic to existing TCP even though the target node has been marked unheathly.  

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1) Setup any service (e.g., nginx ingress), tolerated/tainted to node group A. Use loadbalancer with external traffic policy: cluster. 
2) Scale node pool B. 
3) Simulate many http requests, targetting loadbalancer endpoint of service created in step 1
4) Scale down node pool B.
5) Observe errors on requests that proxied through scaled down node in node pool B.

items.body:
### Describe the issue

### What would you like to be added?

DaemonSet/Deployment supports controlling strategy for scaling pods similar to RollingUpdate.

### Why is this needed?

Currently, DaemonSets and Deployments (via ReplicaSets) offer some level of strategy control for rolling updates, but provide almost nothing for large-range scaling, apart from limiting the request pressure for the API server. As a result, a large number of creating pods will compete simultaneously for the same resources, leading to repeated failures and retries, and very slowly scaling. 

In terms of pod scaling for DaemonSets/Deployments, the current solutions are based on various Autoscalers, but using Autoscalers to achieve specific-number scaling goals might also be inconsistent and awkward:
​	•	For Deployments, scaling relies on the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA).
​	•	For DaemonSets, scaling, that is node scaling,ctypically using the Cluster Autoscaler with Node Pools/Groups and HorizontalNodeScalingPolicy.
However, Node Pools/Groups depend on cloud provider supporting, unusable in local self-built Kubernetes clusters where manual node scaling via adding/removing labels/taints is common.

Additionally, the rolling update strategy for DaemonSets/Deployments is not flexible. It only supports a single fixed updating rate, whereas production environments often require a phased updating strategy of starting slowly and accelerating later.

Support Request also: [English Version](https://discuss.kubernetes.io/t/feature-request-fine-grained-scaling-control-for-daemonsets-deployments/30759?u=unilinu)  [中文版本](https://discuss.kubernetes.io/t/daemonset-deployment/30760)

### What happened?

We use Argo Rollouts to perform canary deployments of our services. During a canary deployment, new pods are brought up (the canary pods) which are included in the [Status](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5ba2b78eae18645744b51d94d279582bdcccec23/pkg/apis/autoscaling/types.go#L51) of the Rollout's scale subresource. When HPA is configured to scale on a metric with a high utilization ratio (generally memory), this results in HPA scaling out, despite the fact that the utilization is under the target. 

This seems to be a result of the behaviour of the [replica calculator](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L65) where:
- the recommended replicas is a simple function of utilizationRatio and the total number of pods returned by the selector
- missing pods with a utilization ratio of below 1 are assumed to be because of a "scale down" and are treated as if they are [consuming 100% of resources](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5ba2b78eae18645744b51d94d279582bdcccec23/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L108-L113) (whereas in this case we are scaling out during a rollout)

In addition, the utilization ratio is never checked prior to updating prior to HPA increasing the desired replicas leading to [incorrect/misleading log messages](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5ba2b78eae18645744b51d94d279582bdcccec23/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L857-L859) like "New size: X; reason: memory resource utilization (percentage of request) above target". 

Further details can be found in issues logged for Argo Rollouts [here](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-rollouts/issues/2857) and [here](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-rollouts/issues/3849).

### What did you expect to happen?

HPA should not scale up when utilization is below target (I.e. when `utilizationRatio < 1`)

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The issue can be reproduced by simulating the behaviour of Argo Rollouts and creating a 2nd `ReplicaSet` with selectors that match an existing `Deployment`. For example:

``` yaml
  template:

    spec:
      containers:

          name: nginx
          resources:

---

metadata:
  name: nginx
  namespace: test
spec:
  maxReplicas: 50
  minReplicas: 3
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: nginx
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: memory
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 50
```

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

DaemonSet/Deployment supports controlling strategy for scaling pods similar to RollingUpdate.

### Why is this needed?

Currently, DaemonSets and Deployments (via ReplicaSets) offer some level of strategy control for rolling updates, but provide almost nothing for large-range scaling, apart from limiting the request pressure for the API server. As a result, a large number of creating pods will compete simultaneously for the same resources, leading to repeated failures and retries, and very slowly scaling. 

In terms of pod scaling for DaemonSets/Deployments, the current solutions are based on various Autoscalers, but using Autoscalers to achieve specific-number scaling goals might also be inconsistent and awkward:
​	•	For Deployments, scaling relies on the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA).
​	•	For DaemonSets, scaling, that is node scaling,ctypically using the Cluster Autoscaler with Node Pools/Groups and HorizontalNodeScalingPolicy.
However, Node Pools/Groups depend on cloud provider supporting, unusable in local self-built Kubernetes clusters where manual node scaling via adding/removing labels/taints is common.

Additionally, the rolling update strategy for DaemonSets/Deployments is not flexible. It only supports a single fixed updating rate, whereas production environments often require a phased updating strategy of starting slowly and accelerating later.

Support Request also: [English Version](https://discuss.kubernetes.io/t/feature-request-fine-grained-scaling-control-for-daemonsets-deployments/30759?u=unilinu)  [中文版本](https://discuss.kubernetes.io/t/daemonset-deployment/30760)

Closes [community kubernetes/kubernetes#129601](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129601)

/sig autoscaling

## What

HPA's development has not been active recently.
It causes many PRs to struggle to get reviews, including some KEPs.
Essentially, this is the problem of lacking approvers in HPA.

## Context (AFAIK)

Currently, @mwielgus is the only approver, but already left the sig-autoscaling chair, and I'm not sure if they're still willing to help in reviewing.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/OWNERS#L7
I know the step down doesn't always mean a stop working on things, but, in this case, actually the last review from them was more than 1 year ago.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pulls?q=is%3Apr+reviewed-by%3Amwielgus+is%3Aclosed

There are some minor changes made in HPA though, all of them are approved by someone else (root approvers), not stamps from sig-autoscaling.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commits/master/pkg/controller/podautoscaler

Also, @gjtempleton is trying to take over the position, and he's (only) a reviewer (not yet approver) apart from @mwielgus now.

- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124661

## Proposal

We're trapped in a vicious cycle; HPA development is not active because of the lack of reviewers/approvers, and no reviewer is newly born because HPA development is not active.

There's (probably, AFAIK) no other active person who is eligible for the reviewer/approver of HPA based on [the official criteria](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/community-membership.md). 
But, we shouldn't keep the current situation, and I'd propose having some volunteers to join reviewers/approvers to break through (even if they're not officially eligible).

Regarding the approver, I cannot come up with any idea other than asking @gjtempleton to be an approver and start approving some PRs. (... I know they're also busy though)

**Which component are you using?**: Horizontal workload autoscaler. **What version of the component are you using?**: Not relevant. **What k8s version are you using (`kubectl version`)?**:
kubectl version Output
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.30.6-dispatcher
Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3
Server Version: v1.30.5-gke.1443001
**What environment is this in?**: Not relevant. **What did you expect to happen?**: When the horizontal autoscaler computes the expected number of replicas, [it uses the following formula](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cf480a3a1a9cb22f3439c0a7922822d9f67f31b5/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L369): ```go usageRatio := float64(usage) / (float64(targetUsagePerPod) * float64(statusReplicas)) ``` (This formula (or a variation of it) appears a couple of times in [this file](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cf480a3a1a9cb22f3439c0a7922822d9f67f31b5/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L369).) It's not impossible that `statusReplicas` (i.e. the `status.replicas` field of the `/scale` subresource) equals zero (e.g. if a user kills pods), leading to a division by zero. [The Golang spec allows divisions by zero to trigger traps](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/43577), although most implementations would return +Inf (which leads to the correct behaviour) or NaN (if `usage == 0.`, in which case the func would return a negative number of replicas). **What happened instead?**: This problem could lead to a panic, or an incorrect behaviour. This could only happen as a result of a race condition, and in the unlikely situation where `status.replicas == 0`. I'm not sure of its practical significance. **How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**: This issue only appears as a result of a race condition. I couldn't produce it.

### What happened?

The setup:
I am using keda with the prometheus scaler. The query I am using, returns the lag in the message queue i am using, and the threshold is set to `0.1`.

What happened:
The lag was increasing for a long time, and the replica count reached the max setting as expected. Everything was running fine for some time. When the lag value reached `214,748,364` hpa decided to reduce the replicas from the max limit to `1`.

### What happened?

In a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) environment, a pod was requesting a large Persistent Volume Claim (PVC). After the appropriate node was identified for the pod, the pod became stuck in the prebinding stage for several minutes while the volume provisioning process completed.  Since the node name was not assigned to the pod during this time, the Cluster Autoscaler perceived the node as unoccupied. Consequently, the Cluster Autoscaler initiated a scale-down of the node, unaware that the pending pod was scheduled to run there.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect that the Scheduler would communicate the intended binding of the pod to the identified node. This would enable the Cluster Autoscaler to recognize that the node is not actually empty and prevent it from being scaled down prematurely.

The issue arose in a large GKE cluster with pods requesting substantial PVCs, making replication potentially challenging. However, the race condition within the Scheduler is evident.

items.body:
### What happened?

When an HPA targets a Deployment which has a label selector matching Pods that don't belong to it (overlapping labels, for example), those "other" Pods are considered by the HPA to be part of the targeted HPA.

### What did you expect to happen?

I have always been lead to believe that this behaviour is correct and the user should have labels that are specific enough to not overlap other Deployments.
This is stated [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#creating-a-deployment):
> Do not overlap labels or selectors with other controllers (including other Deployments and StatefulSets). Kubernetes doesn't stop you from overlapping, and if multiple controllers have overlapping selectors those controllers might conflict and behave unexpectedly.

However, recently the VPA fixed the same behaviour in https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler/pull/6460

Which makes me wonder if I should expect the HPA to test the owner reference too, and only target that Deployment's pods.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create 2 deployments, both with the same labels/selectors
2. In 1 Deployment set resources
3. Deploy an HPA (and metrics-server)
4. Watch the events of the HPA throw error events related to Pods not under control of the HPA's deployment
   1. ie: `  Warning  FailedGetResourceMetric       87s (x3 over 117s)     horizontal-pod-autoscaler  failed to get cpu utilization: missing request for cpu in container ubuntu of Pod other-64886557cb-ldtnt`

  ```yaml
spec:
  ```

items.body:
/sig apps
/sig scheduling
/kind feature
/assign

Want to get feedback on this proposal. I can proceed to KEP process later, if it looks worthy for it to everyone.

## Summary

Refactor Replicaset scaling down implementation for better extendability,
and take Inter-pod scheduling constraints into account during scaling down.

## Motivation

When scaling down happens, the replicaset controller determines Pod(s) to remove based on starting time etc ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L826  )), but not scheduling constraints.

Inter-Pod scheduling constraints (PodAffinity/PodTopologySpread) depend on other Pods’ placement, but they’re honored only at the scheduling time.
It’d be more awesome if we can, at least, keep spreading or affinity _to some extent_ during scaling down in a vanilla kubernetes, that is, without installing [descheduler](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/descheduler) etc. 
Actually, we’ve seen _many_ issues hoping this feature; the oldest one as far as I found is https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/4301!

## Goal

- Refactor the replicaset controller implementation around scaling down and make it easier to implement any scaling down behavior.
  - Introduce `ScaleDownScorePlugin`/`ScaleDownNormalizeScorePlugin` interface and each scaling down factor is implemented as a plugin.
- Take Inter-pod scheduling constraints into account during replicaset scaling down.
  - Inter-pod scheduling constraints are only PodAffinity and PodTopologySpread for now.

## Non Goal

This proposal doesn't mean -
- Always honor those scheduling constraints during scaling down.
  - It'll just be best-effort.
- Take ALL Pods in a cluster into consideration when calculating the best Pod to remove.
  - If we did that, it'd be huge calculation cost.
- Take custom plugins into consideration.
  - Technically, it'd be possible to allow custom `ScaleDownScorePlugin`/`ScaleDownNormalizeScorePlugin` from users, like the scheduling framework does. But, that's out-of-scope in this proposal.

(An elaborated explanation of these Non Goal: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/124306#issuecomment-2054245124)

## Proposal

We’ll introduce a new interface named `ScaleDownScorePlugin`/`ScaleDownNormalizeScorePlugin`.

```go
type ScaleDownScorePlugin interface {
  // Score scores Pods; The higher score a Node gets, the more preferable to remove the Node, from this plugin’s pov.
  // candidatesToDelete is Pods from the replicaset, which the replicaset controller is scaling down.
  // relatedPods is all pods that are owned by any ReplicaSets that is owned by the ReplicaSet's owner.
  // ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go#L796 
  //
  // Each plugin’s Score() is executed concurrently.
  Score(ctx context.Context, candidatesToDelete []*v1.Pod, relatedPods []*v1.Pod) ([]*PodWithScore, error)
}

type ScaleDownNormalizeScorePlugin interface {
  // NormalizeScore is called after all ScaleDownScorePlugin Score() are called. 
  // A successful run of NormalizeScore will update the scores list.
  // Each plugin's NormalizeScore() is executed one by one.
  // candidatesToDelete is the aggregated result from all Score plugins.
  NormalizeScore(ctx context.Context, candidatesToDelete []*PodWithScore) error
}

type PodWithScore struct {
  Pod *v1.Pod
  TotalScore int64
}
```

1. Calculate how many Pods should be removed in the same Replicaset.
2. Call `Score` of each plugin concurrently.
3. Call `NormalizeScore` of each plugin one by one.
4. Remove Pods with higher score.

### How each plugin is implemented

We’ll implement plugins for PodAffinity / PodTopologySpread ( / [existing logic](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L826) to determine which Pods to delete).
 
Each implementation would be like the following:

#### PodAffinity

It'll be implemented as `ScaleDownScorePlugin`.
It gives a high score to candidate Pod if a Node that the candidate Pod is running on doesn’t have a Pod matching PodAffinity of the candidate Pod.
In order to lower the cost of calculation, it’s probably better to use the scheduler’s [snapshot](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cae35dba5a3060711a2a3f958537003bc74a59c0/pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/snapshot.go#L29) in the replicaset controller too.

#### PodTopologySpread

It'll be implemented as `ScaleDownNormalizeScorePlugin`.

1. Group relatedPods based on domain of topology spread
2. Calculate the total score of all Pods’ TotalScore in each domain.
3. Normalize the scores so that each domain’s total score would be similar. 

**Example:** 

Before PodTopologySpread `NormalizeScore()`:

| Domain-a (total: 600) | Domain-b (total: 300) | Domain-c (total: 3000) |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| PodA: 100 | PodD: 100 | PodG: 500 |
| PodB: 200 | PodE: 100 | PodH: 1000 |
| PodC: 300 | PodF: 100 | PodI: 1500 |


After PodTopologySpread `NormalizeScore()`:

| Domain-a (total: 300) | Domain-b (total: 300) | Domain-c (total: 300) |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| PodA: 50 | PodD: 100 | PodG: 50 |
| PodB: 100 | PodE: 100 | PodH: 100 |
| PodC: 150 | PodF: 100 | PodI: 150 |

Before PodTopologySpread, all Pods from Domain-c could be removed, but afterwards it’s not likely that all Pods from the same domain are removed. 

When actually implementing it, we can consider more; for example, in above case, if the controller is trying to remove 5 Pods, all Pods in domain-b could be removed at the same time. So, maybe we want to avoid "all Pods have the same score" after the normalization. (e.g., change to PodD:99 PodE:100 PodF:101)

#### Existing sorting logic

And also note that [existing logic](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L826) to determine which Pod(s) to remove (starting time, deletion-cost, etc) can be also implemented as ScaleDownScorePlugin.

## Risk(Downside) and Mitigation

### Negative impact to throughput of replicaset controller

Scaling down would be slower than the current implementation because of an additional calculation.

I believe it's not the hard/critical requirement to keep the current throughput of scaling **down**.
But, also, given the controller has workers that are run concurrently and are shared between scaling up/scaling down processes, we cannot say there'd be zero impact on scaling up throughput. 

We have to make sure whether the throughput (both scale up and down) is really acceptable after the implementation change.

### Backwards compatibility

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/124306#issuecomment-2077893254

> How will the new scores interact with pod-deletion-cost?

> What about backwards-compatibility? What if users are currently relying on the fact that the first Pod to be deleted is roughly the newest one?

If we just implement the proposal and make it the default behavior, we would break an existing scaling-down behavior.

If we concern about such breaking by this proposal, we can do, for example,

1. add a new field (or annotation) somewhere to make this behaviour non-default.
2. simplify PodTopologySpread's NormalizeScore() and make the scores returned from PodAffinity smaller than other existing algorithm's plugins.
    - simplify PodTopologySpread's NormalizeScore() > e.g., modify only scores of one Pod per domain so that at least one Pod will remain per domain.

I'd prefer (1). If we choose (2), the benefit from this proposal would be small.

## Alternative

Somehow use `controller.kubernetes.io/pod-deletion-cost`, but in anyways, we'd likely end up having to update Pods frequently and I didn't choose that way. 

> Users deploy controllers that update the annotation frequently causing a significant load on the api server. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-apps/2255-pod-cost#risks-and-mitigations

(An elaborated explanation why I didn't choose deletion-cost idea: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/124306#issuecomment-2071237138)

## Reference

- [Current implementation of picking Pods when scaling down](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cae35dba5a3060711a2a3f958537003bc74a59c0/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go#L822-L832)
